In their apartment in Buenos Aires, Valentina started keeping count without meaning to.

Jin used to kiss the back of her neck when he passed the stove. Now he said "smells good" from the doorway. He used to ask about the difficult client at her studio; now he said "how was work?" and nodded at whatever she answered. After dinner he took his laptop to the balcony, and she sat with a book on the sofa, reading the same paragraph.

Separate evenings. Every evening.

She had lived alone for years before him and had never felt this lonely. Alone, at least, no one was sitting ten feet away.

On Thursday she almost said it: "Jin, are we okay?" She got as far as his name. He looked up. She said, "Nothing. Do you want tea?"

He said yes. She made it. The question stayed in her throat.

qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: Why does Valentina feel lonelier now than when she lived alone?
qa.a: She feels lonely and unseen inside the relationship, because Jin is close by but no longer curious about her or affectionate.

qa.q: What could Valentina try instead of offering tea?
qa.a: She could gently say what she has noticed, fewer touches and separate evenings, and ask Jin how he feels, even though it is hard.

qa.q: What might Jin be experiencing when he looks up at his name?
qa.a: He may sense something is coming and feel uneasy, or he may be absorbed in his own worries and not notice the distance at all.

grounding: Valentina notices fewer touches, less curiosity and separate evenings with Jin, feels lonelier than when single, yet says nothing to avoid a hard talk.

Rehana and Tanvir both worked at the same hospital in Lucknow, she in paediatrics, he in radiology, and for three years they had eaten lunch together in the staff canteen every day they could.

These days Tanvir ate at his desk. "Backlog," he said.

At home he was polite, even kind. But he no longer asked about the children on her ward, whose names he used to know. When she came to bed, he was already asleep, or pretending to be. On Sunday he went cycling alone.

On Tuesday Rehana saw him in the canteen after all, laughing with two colleagues over chai. He waved at her. She waved back and sat at a different table.

She was surrounded by people all day. She had never felt so alone.

That night she opened her mouth to say something, then closed it. A hard conversation felt worse than the loneliness. For now.

Varun, you asked how Rakesh uncle and I got through that bad patch, years ago. Your Indu aunty will tell you, because it might help you now.

We'd been married four years. Nothing was wrong exactly. We just didn't talk anymore. He watched cricket, I read. We were like two lodgers.

One night I sat on the edge of the bed and said, "Rakesh, I feel we are drifting. And I don't know how to bring us back." My voice shook.

He put the remote down. He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I've felt it too. I thought you were happier this way."

That was the turning point. We went to a counsellor for a few months. It wasn't magic. But we started talking again.

Saying it out loud didn't fix anything, Varun. It just let us choose.

The train to Farida's parents' town was four hours late, and the waiting room at Itarsi junction was packed. There was nowhere to go and nothing to do. Maybe that was why Farida finally said it.

Arif was scrolling on his phone beside her, as he had been all week, all month.

"Arif," she said. He looked up. "I feel we're drifting. I don't know how to bring us back."

His thumb stopped. Around them, a child cried, a vendor shouted "chai, chai."

"Here?" he said. "Now?"

"We're never anywhere else. We're always busy. This is the first time we've had four hours."

He put the phone in his pocket. "I thought it was just me who felt it."

They talked in low voices while the station roared around them. Not about blame. About whether to try, and how. Maybe a counsellor. Maybe not. But they were talking.

For three months after Vikas and Sarika agreed to try, they did everything the counsellor suggested. Sunday walks in Lodhi Garden. No phones at dinner. A question each night.

Some evenings were good. They laughed like before. Other evenings felt like homework.

One Sunday, walking back past the tombs, Sarika asked herself the question she had been avoiding. Did she want to fix this because she loved Vikas? Or because she was scared of being thirty and alone, of telling her mother, of the empty flat?

She didn't know. That frightened her.

At home she said, "Can I ask you something honest? Are you staying because you want to, or because leaving feels worse?"

Vikas stared at his tea. "Sometimes one. Sometimes the other."

It was the most honest thing either of them had said in months.

Manoj and I gave it four months. We made a deal: honest effort, then an honest decision.

We tried hard. Weekly counselling. Cooking together. A trip to Ooty in October where, for two days, it felt like the beginning again.

But in December I caught myself doing something ugly in my head. When Manoj was kind to me, I felt guilty instead of happy. Like I owed him staying, because he was trying so hard. Because his mother liked me. Because we'd already told everyone we were fine.

That's not love. That's guilt.

I also asked myself if I wanted to leave only because I was bored. I honestly didn't think so. The boredom had been there for a year; the feeling that we were strangers was newer and deeper.

I told Manoj this in January. He cried. So did I. But we both knew it was true.

— Chandrika

Baljeet and Kiran had agreed to part in October. The hard part was that Diwali was in two weeks, and both families expected them at his parents' house in Amritsar.

They sat at the kitchen table in their Delhi flat with a notebook, the same way they used to plan holidays.

"What do we tell them?" Kiran asked.

"The truth, but the same truth. 'We tried, we've grown apart, and we're parting as friends.' No stories about who did what."

"Your mother will ask what I did."

"And I'll say you did nothing wrong. Because you didn't."

They divided the rest: the sofa to her, the books by who bought them, the plant they'd raised together to whoever had more light.

When they finished, Kiran laughed and cried at once. "Is it strange that I feel relieved and sad?"

"No," Baljeet said. "I feel both too."

The school bus had broken down outside Aurangabad on the way back from the science exhibition, and all of Class 10 was stuck on the roadside for an hour.

Imran was handing out water bottles when he saw Farida, his girlfriend of two months, sitting on the milestone with Rehan from the other section. Rehan said something, and Farida threw her head back and laughed, the big laugh Imran thought was only for him.

His stomach clenched like a fist.

She likes him more. The thought arrived fully formed, before he'd even heard what the joke was.

He stood there holding three water bottles, his face hot. He wanted to walk over. He wanted to walk away.

Then Farida looked up, saw him, and waved him over. "Imran! Rehan's telling the story of Sir falling in the pond!"

The fist in his stomach loosened, a little. Not all the way.

You said write it down if it's eating me. So here.

On Friday I saw Jasnoor sitting with Arsh in the library. She was smiling. Since then I've replayed it maybe a hundred times. Was she leaning towards him? Was the smile the special one?

Jasleen went to her cousin's birthday. Nandini was there, and a bunch of boys from her cousin's school. Jasleen posted one group photo. That's all.

I'm Tashi. You asked how things went wrong with Dolma, so I'll tell you straight. I thought I was being a good boyfriend. I really did.

You want to know what it felt like? I'm Nirmala. And the honest answer is, I didn't notice it happening.

Tanvir didn't like my friends. He never said "stop seeing them." He just sulked for hours when I went out with them. So I went out less. Then I stopped going to the art club, because a senior he didn't like was in it.

I felt guilty all the time. If my phone buzzed, my heart jumped, even if it was just my mother. I started saying sorry for things I hadn't done.

One evening my mother asked why I never drew anymore. I burst into tears and told her everything, right there in the kitchen.

She didn't shout. She held me and said, "Loving someone should not make your world smaller." That night she helped me list the things I'd given up. It was a long list.

The next day I went back to art club.

I didn't expect Wilson, of all people, to be the one who got it.

We were on the terrace after tuition, and I was going on about Lavanya again. How she'd laughed with the new boy in her dance class. How she took forty minutes to reply. How I'd asked to see her messages and she'd gone quiet.

Wilson let me talk. Then he said, "Santosh, what are you actually afraid of losing?"

I opened my mouth to say "her". What came out was, "I'm not good enough for her. She's going to figure it out."

It was so quiet I could hear the pigeons.

Wilson said, "So checking her phone is you trying to fix that?"

I realised it was. And it couldn't. Nothing I found in her phone would make me feel good enough. That problem was mine, not hers.

That night, for the first time, I didn't text Lavanya asking who she was with.

Jagdish waited for Radha by the banyan tree near the village school, where they always met on the way home. His cousin Kishore bhaiya had talked with him the night before, on the charpai under the stars, for a long time.

When Radha came, Jagdish didn't ask who she'd been talking to at the well. He'd asked that every day for a month.

Radha looked at him carefully. "You'll stop asking who I talk to?"

"I'll stop. And if I can't, Kishore bhaiya says I should talk to Masterji about it. He's helped other boys."

Radha was quiet. Then she handed him half her roasted corn. "Okay. We'll see."

It wasn't forgiveness yet. But it was a start.
